1.pericope_label: I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand. Then said I, Whither goest thou? And he said unto me, To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof. And, behold, the angel that talked with me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him, And said unto him, Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein: For I, saith the Lord, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that the man with the measuring line is an angel at all, since he has no message and no mission, and calls him a mere figure in the vision implicitly rebuked for what he is doing; he takes the young man to be that same measurer rather than the prophet, insists that the speaker of the fourth verse is the second angel and not the interpreter, and guards the promise of a wall of fire from being made an argument against building, since walls were in fact built not long after. Keil and Delitzsch argue at length that the young man must be the prophet, since the answer is an announcement to carry to the people rather than anything the measurer needed, and refuse the suggestion that the title slights his inexperience.

Gill notes that a Jewish commentator allows the vision to refer to the days of the Messiah while granting it might also encourage those then present about a literal rebuilding, and on the wall of fire pursues the natural history for its own sake, gathering from an ancient writer and two modern travellers that lions fear fire above all things yet will sometimes outbrave it and leap into the fold. Calvin makes the man an angel appearing in human form and explains why such a being is called a man at all, angels putting on that form only for a time and never, strictly speaking, becoming men.

Clarke thinks the man a representation of the cup-bearer who afterwards had commission to build the walls, cites a historian for the fulfilment of the promise of increase, that the city overflowing with inhabitants extended beyond its walls, and states the wall of fire plainly, that her safety consists in the divine defence, though much must refer to a city yet to come. Wesley reads the promise of the suburbs as covering extent and safety alike, identifies the interpreting angel with Christ, and reduces the second half of the fifth verse to a sentence, that the divine presence and favour make her glorious.

Henry identifies the man with Christ, the master builder of his church, who builds exactly by line and level; he turns the young man's youth into an argument, that the prophet entered on his office young and no man ought to despise that; he distinguishes this measuring line from the line of confusion and from the line stretched out for destruction; and he reads the promise as a city lost in its own suburbs, extended as freely as if it had no walls and yet as safe as if it had the strongest.

debates.question: Who is the man with the measuring line?

positions.position: An angel appearing in human form.
Christ himself, the master builder of the church.
A representation of the cup-bearer who later had commission to build the walls.
No angel at all, but a mere figure in the vision, implicitly rebuked.

debates.question: Who is the young man who is to be told the answer?

positions.position: The prophet, since the answer is an announcement to carry to the people and not what the measurer needed.
The man with the measuring line, which gives a much more definite turn to the vision.
The prophet, addressed through the angel and bidden to hasten.

outliers.claim: Pursues the figure of the wall of fire into natural history for its own sake, gathering from an ancient writer and two modern travellers that lions fear fire above all things, and yet that they will sometimes outbrave every such terror and leap into the fold to drag away a sheep.

themes: I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand.
Then said I, Whither goest thou? And he said unto me, To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof.
And, behold, the angel that talked with me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him,
And said unto him, Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein:
For I, saith the Lord, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.

6.pericope_label: Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north, saith the Lord: for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the Lord. Deliver thyself, O Zion, that dwellest with the daughter of Babylon. For thus saith the Lord of hosts; After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye. For, behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants: and ye shall know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out two possible tenses for the verb rendered spread abroad: taken as a past it means scattered and refers to dispersions already made, the exiles being settled by then over a hundred provinces and more; taken as a prophetic perfect it means God has fixed his intention to spread them abroad. He rejects a third rendering, that God will scatter them to the four winds in some new dispersion, as resting on a linguistic error, notes that the ancient Greek paraphrased the other way, takes the daughter of Babylon for that city's inhabitants, and reads the phrase after the glory as meaning in search of glory. Keil and Delitzsch render the run of verses through.

Gill notes that the doubled cry is repeated to confirm the call, as a Jewish commentator observes, takes the speaker of the eighth verse to be Christ, the true Jehovah, as his being sent shows, and says the destruction of the nations needs no more than the bare shaking of a hand.

Clarke identifies the land of the north as Babylonia and the regions round it, prints at length a correspondent's argument that the phrase after the glory should be rendered the future glory and the passage taken as a prophecy of the Messiah, observes on the apple of the eye that anyone looking into another's eye sees his own image in miniature in the pupil, and has the threat come first and the stroke after. Wesley calls the doubled cry an address to sleepy men and states the balance without the grammar, that as the threat was executed in scattering them so the promise will be performed in gathering them.

Henry alone explains why a second summons was needed: the proclamation of Cyrus might have brought them all back, yet only some forty thousand went, the land of their captivity being to most of them the land of their birth, where they had taken root and some had got estates. He traces the refusal to distrust of the promise and love of ease, notes the harm done to those who had gone, and explains the odd phrase that Zion dwells with the daughter of Babylon, since many of her sons dwelt in that city and where the people of God are the church of God is.

debates.question: What does the clause about spreading abroad mean?

positions.position: Either a past scattering already accomplished or a prophetic perfect of an intended spreading; a third rendering, a new dispersion still to come, rests on a linguistic error.
The threat and the promise balanced: as the scattering executed the threat, the gathering performs the promise.
The scattering was owned to be in wrath, so the invitation is a token of willingness to be reconciled.

debates.question: How should the phrase after the glory be rendered?

positions.position: As the future glory, or the glory that is to come, making the passage a prophecy of the Messiah.
As in search of glory, to display God's glory on the heathen by first breaking their power and afterwards attaching them to his service.
The speaker is Christ, the true Jehovah, as his being sent shows.

outliers.claim: Supplies documentary evidence for the troubles that overtook Babylon, a great rock inscription cut by Darius recording two insurrections in Babylonia and the taking of the city twice, by the king himself and by his general.

themes: Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north, saith the Lord: for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the Lord.
Deliver thyself, O Zion, that dwellest with the daughter of Babylon.
For thus saith the Lord of hosts; After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye.
For, behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants: and ye shall know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me.

10.pericope_label: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and shall be my people: and I will dwell in the midst of thee, and thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto thee. And the Lord shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again. Be silent, O all flesh, before the Lord: for he is raised up out of his holy habitation.

schools.summary: Ellicott agrees that the promise of indwelling was meant first of the second temple, but adds that the visible manifestation was never given there again and calls the later fulfilment one little dreamt of by the prophet; he collects the variants of the ancient Greek at the eleventh verse, notes that the words about the sending imply a fulfilment near enough to prove the speaker's commission, observes that the holy land occurs here only, and admits that the promise has not been literally fulfilled. Keil and Delitzsch ground the twelfth verse on the older passage where the nation is called the Lord's portion, and take the name for the delivered remnant gathered out of Babel.

Gill follows the Targum in reading the daughter of Zion as the congregation of Zion, expects a return of the believing Jews to their own land, and takes the command to be silent for astonishment at the work, so that none dare open his mouth against it, reporting that the Targum turns the words on the wicked.

Clarke refers the indwelling chiefly to the Christian church, in which God dwells by his Spirit as he had once by a symbol, says roundly that no nation ever became converts to the Jewish religion whereas whole nations have embraced the faith of Christ, reads a final restoration in the twelfth verse, and has the nations amazed as God arises to deliver an ancient people. Wesley divides the indwelling evenly between the Jews and the gospel church, glosses the inheriting as to claim, recover and delight in as a man does in a paternal inheritance, and makes the silence reverence and expectation at once.

Henry sets the summons to sing against the circumstances of those who first heard it, the returned Jews being in distress with spiteful neighbours and cool brethren, and holds that those who have recovered purity and liberty may sing before they recover prosperity. He gives the promise of indwelling two accomplishments, the temple worship and the incarnation, and holds that the nation multiplied greatly by proselytes after the captivity, naturalized and entitled to all the privileges of native Israelites, which he reads as an earnest of the calling of the Gentiles.

debates.question: Did any nation ever join itself to the God of Israel before Christ?

positions.position: No nation or people ever became converts to the Jewish religion; whole nations have embraced the faith of Christ.
The nation multiplied greatly by proselytes after the captivity, perhaps equal in number to the native Israelites, and that was an earnest of the calling of the Gentiles.

debates.question: How far is the promise that God will inherit Judah in the holy land fulfilled?

positions.position: Not literally at all: the coming of Christ was the beginning of the rejection of that people and the destruction of their city.
A promise of the final restoration of the Jews to their own land.
Fulfilled in the delivered remnant gathered out of Babel to dwell on holy ground as the Lord's portion.

outliers.claim: Does not treat the failure of literal fulfilment as damaging to the prophet, holding that the prophets saw only as in a mirror and that no one of them received the truth entire.

themes: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the Lord.
And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and shall be my people: and I will dwell in the midst of thee, and thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto thee.
And the Lord shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again.
Be silent, O all flesh, before the Lord: for he is raised up out of his holy habitation.
